results.claim: For d=δ⁺(D)≥1, a directed cycle of length at least d+1 can be found in polynomial time; additionally, n<d+k is an immediate sound NO condition. Thus the target is completely solved for k=1.
results.proof_sketch: Greedily extend a simple directed path P=v₁…v_p until v_p has no out-neighbor outside P. All at least d out-neighbors of v_p therefore occur among v₁,…,v_{p−1}. If v_i is the earliest one, then d≤p−i, and v_i→v_{i+1}→…→v_p→v_i is a directed cycle on p−i+1≥d+1 vertices. The construction is polynomial. Conversely, no cycle has more than n vertices, so n<d+k certifies NO.

results.claim: For any integer L≥2, existence of a directed cycle of length at least L is exactly equivalent to a short-leg two-way linkage, yielding an explicit O(n^L(n+m)) exact algorithm.
results.proof_sketch: Enumerate every ordered L-tuple P=(v₁,…,v_L) of distinct vertices whose consecutive pairs are arcs. Delete v₂,…,v_{L−1} and test whether v_L reaches v₁. A simple return path together with P is a simple directed cycle of length at least L. Conversely, from any cycle of length at least L, take L consecutive vertices for P; the complementary segment is a return path avoiding P's internal vertices. Hence enumeration plus reachability is exact. For the target take L=d+k. This exposes the algorithmic bottleneck: the exponent depends on d+k, so this is not FPT in k.

results.claim: There is a polynomially checkable upper-bound certificate: if X is an independent vertex set and every arc entering X from outside X has its tail in S⊆V(D)\X, then every directed cycle has length at most n−|X|+|S|.
results.proof_sketch: For every x∈X lying on a directed cycle C, its predecessor on C cannot lie in X, since X is independent. By the entering-arc hypothesis that predecessor lies in S. Distinct vertices of C∩X have distinct predecessors, because a cycle vertex has only one successor on C. Thus |C∩X|≤|C∩S|≤|S|. At most n−|X| other vertices occur, proving |C|≤n−|X|+|S|. Therefore n−|X|+|S|<d+k is a verifiable NO certificate.

results.claim: Let D be a bidirected complete multipartite digraph on n vertices, and let d=δ⁺(D). Its circumference is exactly min(n,2d), and a maximum directed cycle can be constructed in polynomial time. If d≥2, then D is 2-strong.
results.proof_sketch: Let M be the size of a largest part. A vertex in that part has outdegree n−M, while every other vertex has at least that outdegree, so d=n−M. On any cycle, vertices from the largest part must be separated by vertices outside it; hence the cycle has length at most both n and 2(n−M)=2d. If M>d, list all d outside vertices and alternate them with d vertices of the largest part, obtaining a 2d-cycle. If M≤d, place the M largest-part vertices cyclically as separators. Make M bins for the intervening gaps. Assign the vertices of each other part injectively to distinct bins, always filling empty bins first. Each such part has size at most M, and there are d≥M outside vertices, so every bin becomes nonempty. Within each bin, vertices come from distinct parts; ordering each bin arbitrarily gives a Hamiltonian directed cycle. All steps are polynomial. Finally, d≥2 ensures that deleting any vertex leaves at least two nonempty parts, whose bidirected cross-arcs make the remainder strong.

results.claim: The target has a polynomial-time solution on bidirected complete multipartite digraphs: such an input is YES exactly when n≥d+k and d≥k.
results.proof_sketch: By the preceding exact circumference formula, a qualifying cycle exists exactly when min(n,2d)≥d+k. This single inequality is equivalent to the conjunction n≥d+k and 2d≥d+k, the latter being d≥k. The preceding construction outputs a maximum cycle whenever the conditions hold; otherwise the formula certifies NO. The multipartition and its validity can be recovered and checked from pairwise adjacency in polynomial time.

results.claim: For every fixed k≥3 there are 2-strong NO-instances of arbitrarily large order satisfying n≥d+k: the bidirected complete bipartite digraph with part sizes 2 and a, for any a≥k, has d=2 and circumference 4=d+2.
results.proof_sketch: This is the preceding construction with two parts. Each vertex in the a-part has outdegree 2 and each vertex in the 2-part has outdegree a, so d=2. Deleting any vertex leaves a nonempty bidirected complete bipartite digraph and hence a strong digraph, so the input is 2-strong. Every directed cycle alternates between the parts and therefore uses at most two vertices from each; a directed 4-cycle exists, so the circumference is exactly 4. For k≥3 and a≥k, n=a+2≥d+k while 4<2+k=d+k. Letting a grow gives arbitrarily large order.

results.claim: For every fixed k≥4 there are 2-strong NO-instances with arbitrarily large minimum outdegree and with n≥d+k; indeed their circumference is exactly d+3.
results.proof_sketch: Let Q be a q-vertex set, q≥3, containing x,y, and let A be an a-vertex set, a≥2. Make Q complete bidirected; add every arc A→Q and every arc {x,y}→A; add no others. Deleting any vertex leaves a strong digraph: the surviving core is complete, every A-vertex reaches it, and at least one of x,y remains to reach all of A. Hence the digraph is 2-strong. Vertices in Q\{x,y} have outdegree q−1, vertices of A have outdegree q, so d=q−1. Every A-vertex on a cycle must be preceded by x or y, so a cycle contains at most two A-vertices and has length at most q+2. For distinct a₁,a₂∈A and an ordering z₁,…,z_{q−2} of Q\{x,y}, the cycle x,a₁,z₁,…,z_{q−2},y,a₂,x has length q+2. Thus the circumference is q+2=d+3. Taking a≥k−1 gives n≥d+k but no cycle of length d+k for k≥4. Consequently, neither large d nor a bounded number of vertices outside a longest cycle can supply the required FPT win condition.

results.claim: The two-gateway example extends exactly as follows. For integers s≥2, q≥s+1, and a≥s, let Q be a bidirected q-vertex clique, let A be an independent a-vertex set, add every arc A→Q, and add arcs from Q to A precisely when their tail belongs to a fixed s-set S⊂Q. Then d=q−1, the strong vertex-connectivity is exactly s, and the circumference is q+s=d+s+1.
results.proof_sketch: Vertices of Q\S have outdegree q−1, vertices of A have outdegree q, and vertices of S have outdegree q−1+a, so d=q−1. After deletion of fewer than s vertices, some gateway in S survives. The surviving vertices of Q form a bidirected clique; every surviving A-vertex reaches Q directly, and every surviving Q-vertex reaches A through the surviving gateway. Hence the remainder is strong. Deleting all of S leaves nonempty Q\S and A but no path from Q\S to A, so the connectivity is exactly s. Apply the predecessor certificate with X=A: only S sends arcs into A, so every cycle has at most s vertices of A and hence at most q+s vertices. For distinct a₁,…,a_s∈A and S={s₁,…,s_s}, traverse s₁,a₁,s₂,a₂,…,s_s,a_s and then all vertices of Q\S before returning to s₁. All required arcs exist, giving a cycle of length q+s.

results.claim: For every k≥3 and h≥0 there is a 2-strong NO-instance whose order and circumference satisfy n=d+k+h and c(D)=d+k−1. For every k≥4 these instances can additionally have arbitrarily large d and strong vertex-connectivity exactly k−2.
results.proof_sketch: For k=3, take the bidirected K_{2,3+h}. It has d=2, n=5+h=d+k+h, and circumference 4=d+k−1. For k≥4, apply the generalized gateway construction with s=k−2, a=k−1+h, and arbitrary q≥k−1. It has d=q−1, n=q+a=d+k+h, connectivity s=k−2≥2, and circumference q+s=d+k−1. Letting q grow makes d unbounded. In particular, h=0 gives n=d+k while the longest cycle has n−1 vertices; arbitrary h shows that even unbounded surplus order need not help. This is an obstruction to order-, degree-, or connectivity-only sufficient conditions, not a parameterized-complexity lower bound.

results.claim: The target has a polynomial-time solution on semicomplete digraphs: such an input is YES exactly when n≥d+k, and a Hamiltonian directed cycle can be constructed when YES.
results.proof_sketch: A semicomplete digraph has at least one arc between every pair. Start with any directed cycle C in the strong input. If an outside vertex z satisfies c_i→z→c_{i+1} for consecutive vertices of C, insert z. If no such insertion exists, scanning cyclically shows every outside z either is dominated by every vertex of C and has no arc to C, or dominates every vertex of C and receives no arc from C: if both kinds of adjacency occurred, a transition around C would give an insertion. Strongness ensures both classes occur and supplies an arc u→v from the C-dominated class to the C-dominating class (take the first class transition on a path to C). Then replace any edge c_i→c_{i+1} by c_i→u→v→c_{i+1}. Repeating constructs a Hamiltonian cycle in polynomial time. A 2-strong digraph is strong, so the result applies. The size condition is necessary and sufficient.

results.claim: Given any baseline cycle C with ℓ=|C|≥d+1, either ℓ≥d+k and C is a target witness, or r=d+k−ℓ satisfies 1≤r≤k−1 and the target reduces exactly to Connected Assignment Augmentation: find a perfect matching whose induced permutation has exactly one nontrivial cycle and at least ℓ+r nonfixed vertices.
results.proof_sketch: Build a bipartite graph with left and right copies of V(D). Include u_Lv_R with weight one for every nonloop arc u→v, and include every diagonal v_Lv_R with weight zero. A perfect matching defines a permutation π: a nonfixed permutation cycle v₁,…,v_t uses arcs v_i→v_{i+1} and is therefore a directed cycle; fixed points are unused vertices. Conversely, a directed cycle H extends to such a perfect matching by using H's successor arcs and diagonal edges elsewhere. Thus matchings with exactly one nontrivial permutation cycle and weight at least ℓ+r correspond exactly to directed cycles of length at least ℓ+r=d+k. The baseline C supplies an incumbent matching of weight ℓ. If it is not already a witness, r>0; since ℓ≥d+1, r≤k−1. Construction and witness transfer are polynomial. This is a parameter-preserving reformulation, not an algorithm for enforcing the one-cycle constraint.

results.claim: For every loopless digraph D, the maximum number p(D) of vertices coverable by pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles is computable in polynomial time by maximum-weight bipartite perfect matching. Moreover c(D)≤p(D), so p(D)<d+k is a sound polynomial-time NO rule.
results.proof_sketch: Use the weighted bipartite graph from the preceding claim. It always has the all-diagonal perfect matching. Every perfect matching is a permutation of V(D); its nonfixed permutation cycles are pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles, and its weight is exactly their total number of vertices. Conversely, any packing of pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles, completed by diagonal edges on uncovered vertices, is a perfect matching of the same weight. Hence maximum matching weight equals p(D). Maximum-weight bipartite perfect matching is polynomial-time computable. A single directed cycle is a valid packing, so c(D)≤p(D), proving the rejection rule. When p(D)≥d+k the test is only inconclusive: the matching may split its weight among several cycles.

results.claim: The cycle-packing bound subsumes every independent-set predecessor certificate from the parent: p(D)≤n−|X|+|S| under that certificate's hypotheses. It is tight on the parent's bidirected complete multipartite, gateway, and strong semicomplete families.
results.proof_sketch: In any cycle packing, map each covered x∈X to its predecessor. Independence puts that predecessor outside X, the entry hypothesis puts it in S, and disjoint cycles make the map injective. Thus at most |S| covered vertices lie in X, while at most n−|X| lie outside, proving the bound on p(D). For a bidirected complete multipartite graph, if 2d<n take X to be a largest part and S=V\X, of size d; then p≤2d, while the parent's cycle attains 2d. If 2d≥n, p≤n and the parent's Hamiltonian cycle attains n. For the gateway graph, X=A and S is the gateway set give p≤q+s, while its exhibited cycle has q+s vertices. A strong semicomplete graph has the parent's Hamiltonian cycle, so c=p=n. Hence p=c on all three families, including their stated NO subfamilies.

results.claim: The one-cycle constraint cannot be discarded even for 2-strong inputs: the bidirected Petersen digraph has d=3 and p(D)=10 but circumference c(D)=9. Consequently, for k=7 it is a NO-instance with n=d+k on which the matching relaxation attains the target threshold.
results.proof_sketch: Use vertices a_i,b_i for i modulo 5, with undirected outer edges a_i a_{i+1}, spokes a_i b_i, and inner edges b_i b_{i+2}, and replace every edge by both arcs. Every vertex has outdegree three. After deleting an a_i, the intact inner 5-cycle connects all remaining outer vertices through their spokes; after deleting a b_i, the intact outer 5-cycle connects all remaining inner vertices. Thus every one-vertex deletion is strong. The five spoke 2-cycles form a packing covering all ten vertices, so p=10. A Hamiltonian cycle would use an even positive number of spokes, hence two or four. With two, its outer restriction and inner restriction would each be a spanning path; the spoke indices would have to differ by both ±1 and ±2 modulo 5, impossible. With four, if spoke t is omitted, the forced outer and inner edges plus the other spokes form two disjoint 5-cycles, not one 10-cycle. Thus c≤9, while a₁,a₂,a₃,a₄,b₄,b₂,b₀,b₃,b₁ is a 9-cycle.

final_writeup:
Let d=δ⁺(D), n=|V(D)|, and c(D) be the circumference. I did not obtain the requested f(k)n^{O(1)} algorithm for arbitrary 2-strong digraphs, so the resolution remains partial. All ten independently verified parent claims are retained.

The constructive baseline still gives a cycle C of length ℓ≥d+1 in polynomial time, settles k=1, and makes n<d+k an immediate NO case. The exact short-leg linkage algorithm runs in O(n^{d+k}(n+m)), not FPT in k. The predecessor lemma remains a checkable upper-bound certificate. The complete multipartite and semicomplete subclasses remain polynomially solvable, while the bipartite and gateway constructions remain sharp 2-strong NO families; in particular, for every k≥3 and h≥0 they realize n=d+k+h and c(D)=d+k−1, with arbitrarily large d and connectivity k−2 when k≥4.

The structural-reformulation lens gives an exact parameter-preserving intermediate problem. Form a bipartite assignment instance with a left and right copy of each vertex, weight-one edges for digraph arcs, and weight-zero diagonal fallback edges. Perfect matchings are permutations. Their nonfixed permutation cycles are precisely packings of vertex-disjoint directed cycles. Requiring exactly one nonfixed cycle makes the correspondence exact for a single directed cycle. The baseline C supplies a one-cycle matching of weight ℓ. If C is short of the target, the required augmentation r=d+k−ℓ lies between 1 and k−1. Thus the original target is exactly Connected Assignment Augmentation by at most k−1 above a supplied feasible one-cycle assignment. A solution matching reconstructs the target cycle directly, and every target cycle supplies such a matching.

Dropping the one-cycle constraint is polynomial: maximum-weight bipartite matching computes p(D), the maximum number of vertices covered by disjoint directed cycles. Since c(D)≤p(D), p(D)<d+k is a sound polynomial NO rule. This bound automatically subsumes every predecessor certificate: for independent X whose entering arcs have tails in S, the predecessor injection works across an entire cycle packing and gives p(D)≤n−|X|+|S|. The relaxation is tight on all audited complete multipartite, gateway, and strong semicomplete families, so it structurally unifies their circumference proofs and certificates.

The relaxation does not solve the connected problem. In the bidirected Petersen digraph, the five spokes give a cycle packing covering all ten vertices, but a parity analysis of spokes rules out a Hamiltonian cycle; an explicit 9-cycle exists. This digraph is 2-strong and has d=3, so at k=7 the matching optimum reaches d+k=10 although the correct answer is NO. Hence an FPT argument must control consolidation into one cycle, not merely total cycle-packing weight.

The reformulation removes d from the augmentation parameter, but it does not provide an f(k)n^{O(1)} method for enforcing the one-cycle constraint. The audited target-coverage judgment therefore remains VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS. The draft still does not settle k=2 or the general arbitrary-input problem.
